claims.text: The relevant initial material is an as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi high-entropy-alloy nanoscale film or patterned nanoribbon on silicon.
The as-deposited material contains nanoscale chemical disorder and grain boundaries.
Poor heat dissipation in FeMnNiGeSi films or nanoribbons produces localized temperature gradients during low-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
Localized temperature gradients generate or aggravate differential thermal stresses at nanoscale grain boundaries.
Stress fields and grain boundaries can impede magnetic-domain-wall motion.
Increased domain-wall pinning raises coercivity and magnetic hysteresis losses.
Thermal bottlenecks cause delayed domain-wall motion through nonuniform local temperatures.
An approximately 5 nm Cu capping layer will enhance interfacial thermal conductance of the FeMnNiGeSi film or nanoribbon.
Enhanced interfacial thermal conductance from the Cu cap will reduce local temperature gradients.
Reducing thermal gradients will alleviate differential thermal stress and domain-wall pinning.
Improved heat extraction will synchronize local temperatures during magnetic-field cycling.
Cu-capped samples will show a more pronounced and sharper magnetocaloric entropy-change peak than uncapped samples.
Cu-capped samples will exhibit narrower M-H loops and thus less hysteresis than uncapped samples.
A comparable inert, low-thermal-conductivity cap will not significantly improve the entropy-change peak or hysteresis.
The proposed operating regime is an applied field below 100 mT, cycling frequency below 1 Hz, and a temperature sweep spanning the magnetic transition.
A Cu cap could introduce interfacial strain or chemical interactions that confound its thermal effect.
The magnitude of the cap-induced thermal-conductance and magnetocaloric changes is not yet known.

Failure of the Cu-capped samples to sharpen the entropy-change peak and reduce hysteresis, or equal improvement from the low-conductivity control cap, would falsify the proposed heat-transfer mechanism.
